props.title: The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie

sections.content: Luis Buñuel's masterpiece The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie revolutionized surrealist cinema by weaponizing dinner party etiquette into biting social satire. The film's genius lies in how it normalizes the absurd - characters repeatedly attempt to dine together but get interrupted by increasingly bizarre circumstances, from military maneuvers to ghost stories. This inspired later surrealist social commentaries like Brazil (1985) and Synecdoche, New York (2008), while its dream-within-a-dream structure directly influenced Inception (2010).

sections.content: The film's influence on satirical surrealism can't be overstated. Its DNA appears in Sorry to Bother You (2018), where corporate capitalism creates increasingly absurd scenarios, and The Lobster (2015), which similarly uses deadpan delivery to normalize bizarre social rules. The way Buñuel weaves dreams and reality created a template for directors like David Lynch, particularly in Mulholland Drive (2001) and Lost Highway (1997).

What sets Buñuel's approach apart is his precise targeting of upper-class pretension. Unlike the broad surrealism of Un Chien Andalou (1929), this film uses the surreal to specifically expose social hypocrisy. Its influence appears in Parasite (2019) and The Square (2017), which similarly use increasingly absurd scenarios to dissect class dynamics. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Surrealist Social Commentary

sections.content: Modern filmmakers continue building on Buñuel's foundation of using surrealism as social critique. Mother! (2017) adopts similar techniques of escalating absurdity, while Triangle of Sadness (2022) directly echoes Buñuel's attack on wealthy diners through extreme circumstances. The film's influence even reaches TV series like Succession (2018-2023), where wealth creates its own bizarre reality.
